passage: I'm Ujjwal. When our friend Nandita got the summer internship at the research lab, two of my roommates reacted in completely different ways, and I've been watching both since. Kishore stuck her acceptance screenshot on his wall and said, "If she did it from our college, I can." He made a list: two projects, one cold email a week. He's at the library by eight now. Salil went the other way. He kept opening her profile, then his own, then closing both. He told me, "She's just smarter. I'm never getting anything like that." He's stopped going to the coding club. I can't see inside either of them. But Kishore looks at Nandita's news like a map, and Salil looks at it like a verdict.

qa.q: What did Kishore stick on his wall?
qa.a: Nandita's acceptance screenshot.

qa.q: What does Salil's "She's just smarter. I'm never getting anything like that" suggest about his state of mind?
qa.a: He seems envious and hopeless, seeing the goal as out of reach, which drains his effort.

qa.q: What small step might help Salil turn the comparison into something useful?
qa.a: He could ask Nandita how she applied and pick one reachable step, like Kishore's weekly email, so the goal feels possible.

qa.q: How might Nandita feel if she knew how differently her news landed?
qa.a: Nandita might be glad to have inspired Kishore and sorry that Salil felt worse, and might want to share how she did it.

grounding: A roommate watches one friend use a peer's internship as motivation while another sinks into envy, depending on whether the goal feels reachable.

passage:
Monday. Urmila posted that she'd got the summer internship at the design firm. Sumit congratulated her, then lay on his hostel bed for an hour thinking, she's better at everything, why do I even bother. He skipped the evening studio.
Thursday. In the canteen he finally asked, "How did you even get it?" Urmila laughed. "Rejected by six places first. Then I redid my portfolio twice with Ma'am's help." Sumit stared. Six rejections. A portfolio. That was... doable.
Two weeks later. Sumit had booked a slot with the same professor and was redoing his first project at midnight, lamp on, reference sheets everywhere. When a friend asked what had changed, he said, "Nothing. I just found out the ladder has steps."

qa.q: How many places rejected Urmila first?
qa.a: Six places.

qa.q: What was Sumit thinking as he lay on his hostel bed on Monday?
qa.a: He was thinking she's better at everything and wondering why he even bothers, sinking into envy.

qa.q: What turned Sumit's comparison from a weight into a push?
qa.a: Learning her real path, six rejections and a redone portfolio, made the goal feel reachable, so he booked a slot and started working 🙂

qa.q: How might Urmila feel about having been honest in the canteen?
qa.a: Urmila may be glad she shared the rejections, since it helped a friend instead of making her success look effortless.

grounding: Over two weeks a student's envy of a friend's internship turns into motivation once he learns the goal is reachable step by step.

passage: Sit, Bhupen. You've been staring at Arpit's promotion email for ten minutes. Your Sabina ma'am was twenty once, you know. In college, my friend Anjum won a scholarship to study abroad. Two of us heard the news the same day. Rosy said, "If Anjum can, so can I," and started writing to universities that week. It took her two years, but she went. Me? I told myself Anjum was simply brilliant and I was ordinary. I stopped applying for anything. I wasted a whole year feeling small. The difference wasn't talent, Bhupen. Rosy saw a road. I saw a wall. Now go and ask Arpit how he prepared. Then decide which one you're looking at.

qa.q: What did Anjum win?
qa.a: A scholarship to study abroad.

qa.q: How did young Sabina feel after hearing Anjum's news?
qa.a: She felt ordinary and small, telling herself Anjum was simply brilliant, and she stopped applying.

qa.q: What is Sabina ma'am suggesting Bhupen do, and why?
qa.a: To ask Arpit how he prepared, so Bhupen can see a road rather than a wall and choose real steps.

qa.q: How might Rosy have seen Anjum's scholarship?
qa.a: Rosy saw it as proof that it was possible for people like them, which pushed her to start writing to universities.

grounding: An elder recalls how the same friend's success spurred one young woman on and pulled another down, depending on whether the goal felt reachable.

passage: The cyclone warning had shut the campus, the hostel generator ran only the corridor lights, and the next internship deadline was midnight tomorrow. By candlelight, Elizabeth read out her acceptance from the marine research station, then apologised for being so happy. Preeti hugged her. Then she lay on her bed in the dark, thinking: of course. Elizabeth is brilliant. I'll never get anything like that. She didn't open her laptop. At ten, Elizabeth sat on the edge of Preeti's bed. "I got rejected by four places first. Want to see my first draft? It was awful." It was. Preeti laughed out loud. Elizabeth's success suddenly looked less like a mountain and more like a staircase. With nineteen percent battery, Preeti opened her own statement and started cutting the first paragraph.

qa.q: How many places rejected Elizabeth first?
qa.a: Four places.

qa.q: What was Preeti thinking as she lay in the dark after the hug?
qa.a: She was sinking into envy and self-doubt, sure that Elizabeth was brilliant and that she herself would never get anything like it.

qa.q: What turned the comparison from crushing to useful?
qa.a: Seeing Elizabeth's four rejections and awful first draft made the goal look reachable, like a staircase, so Preeti opened the laptop and started editing.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth have felt reading out the news beside a friend who was struggling?
qa.a: Elizabeth seemed torn between joy and worry about hurting Preeti, which is why she apologised for being happy and later shared her rejections.

grounding: A student's envy of a friend's internship first stops her working, then turns into motivation once the friend's path looks reachable.

passage: In the college canteen in Dadar, the news went round fast: Rashid had got an articleship at a big audit firm. Gautam and Usha read the message together over cutting chai. Gautam whistled. "He cleared the intermediate one month before us. If he can, we can by March." He started listing firms on a paper napkin. Usha smiled and said nothing. On the local train home she scrolled through Rashid's profile, his neat marks, his confident photo, and felt her stomach drop. Rashid had always been ahead; she had already failed one paper. What was the point? At home she didn't open her books. She re-read the message until the words stopped meaning anything. Next day Gautam waved the napkin at her. "I've marked ten firms. Take five?" Usha looked at the list for a long moment and couldn't answer.

qa.q: What did Gautam write on the paper napkin?
qa.a: A list of firms; he marked ten.

qa.q: Why did Usha feel her stomach drop on the train?
qa.a: She compared herself with Rashid, who had always been ahead, and with one failed paper the goal felt out of reach, so envy slid into self-criticism.

qa.q: When Gautam offers five firms, what small step could help Usha?
qa.a: She could take even one or two firms and make a plan for the failed paper, turning a far-off goal into something she can reach.

qa.q: Why might Gautam and Usha react so differently to the same news?
qa.a: Gautam sees Rashid as just a month ahead, so the goal feels close; Usha, carrying a failed paper, sees the news as proof she is too far behind.

grounding: Two students hear of a friend's articleship; one is spurred on because the goal feels close, while the other sinks into envy because it feels out of reach.

passage: In our second year, our friend Arvind got a summer internship at a big firm in Bengaluru, and Divyansh and I both heard the news in the hostel corridor. I'm Farhan. For me, it was like a punch. I lay on my bed thinking, "I'll never get anything like that. I'm useless." I stopped going to the coding club. I scrolled Arvind's posts every night and felt worse. Divyansh reacted differently. He asked Arvind how he'd prepared, made a list of skills to learn, and started practising two hours every evening. "If Arvind did it, I can too," he said. Watching him, I realised the same news had pushed him forward and pulled me down. The difference was that he saw the goal as reachable. I didn't. Later, I asked Divyansh to show me his list.

qa.q: Where was Arvind's internship?
qa.a: It was at a big firm in Bengaluru.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel after hearing about Arvind's internship?
qa.a: Farhan felt crushed and useless, sinking into envy and self-criticism.

qa.q: What made the same news motivating for Divyansh?
qa.a: Divyansh saw the goal as reachable, asked how Arvind prepared and made a practice plan, turning comparison into action.

qa.q: How might Arvind feel if he knew his news affected his friends so differently?
qa.a: Arvind might be surprised and want to help both, perhaps sharing his preparation tips more openly.

grounding: Two students hear a friend's internship news: one is inspired to work harder, the other sinks into envy, depending on whether the goal seems reachable.

passage:
Mentor's note, Wednesday.
Both Jyoti and Kavitha heard this week that their batchmate got a research fellowship abroad. Their reactions couldn't be more different. Jyoti came to me the next day with a printout of the fellowship requirements. "What do I need to be ready for next year?" We made a plan: one paper, better statistics, two recommendations. Kavitha, on the other hand, has been quiet and skipped the lab twice. When I asked, she said, "What's the point? I'll never be at her level." She seemed to have decided the goal was out of reach. I asked her to write down three small steps she could take this month. She hesitated, but wrote one. I'll check in with both of them next week.

qa.q: What did Jyoti bring to the mentor?
qa.a: Jyoti came with a printout of the fellowship requirements.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling when she said "What's the point?"
qa.a: Kavitha felt discouraged and envious, sure she'd never reach that level.

qa.q: Why might small steps help Kavitha?
qa.a: Breaking the goal into steps makes it feel reachable, which can turn comparison from a weight into motivation.

qa.a: The batchmate likely doesn't know her success is inspiring one friend and discouraging another.

grounding: A mentor sees the same news of a batchmate's fellowship motivate one student and sink another into envy, depending on whether the goal seems reachable.

passage:
Monday
Madhuri got the marketing internship at that agency. The one I applied to and never heard back from. I smiled and hugged her and then went and cried in the washroom.
All evening I kept thinking: she's smarter, prettier, more confident. I'll never get anything.
Tuesday
Still sulking. Skipped the case-study class.
Wednesday
Madhuri told me how she prepared: three mock interviews, rewrote her portfolio twice, and got rejected by four places first. Four!
So she didn't just float in. It's not magic. It's steps.
I made a list: fix portfolio, practise interviews with Madhuri, apply to five places by the end of the month. The envy's still there. But it feels like a direction now, not a hole.
- Vandana

qa.a: Madhuri got rejected by four places first.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel on Monday evening?
qa.a: Vandana felt envious and hopeless, crying in the washroom and thinking success would never come.

qa.q: What changed Vandana's comparison from corrosive to motivating?
qa.a: Learning Madhuri's concrete steps made the goal feel reachable, so Vandana made a plan instead of sulking.

qa.q: How might Madhuri feel helping Vandana practise interviews?
qa.a: Madhuri would likely feel glad and close to Vandana, sharing what helped her.

grounding: A student's envy at a friend's internship first pulls the student down, then turns into motivation once the goal seems reachable.

passage:
In the small town of Satna, cousins Bhavna and Dhruv heard the same news at the Sunday lunch: their neighbour's son had got a paid internship at a Pune software firm.
Bhavna asked him questions all through the meal. "What did you study? Which course online?" She wrote the names on her hand.
Dhruv ate silently. On the terrace later, he said, "I'll never get that. I'm stuck in a college nobody's heard of."
"So's he," said Bhavna. "Same college."
"He's just smarter."
"He said he did two online courses. That's all. We can do that."
Dhruv shrugged and scrolled his phone. Bhavna went downstairs to look up the first course.

qa.q: Where was the neighbour's son's internship?
qa.a: It was at a Pune software firm.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling on the terrace?
qa.a: He felt envious and discouraged, sure he would never get such a chance.

qa.q: What makes Bhavna's reaction helpful to her?
qa.a: She treats the news as a map: she asks about the steps and sees they are reachable, so she starts the first course.

qa.q: What might change for Dhruv if he saw the steps as reachable?
qa.a: He might feel hopeful instead of stuck, and start working toward something like it.

grounding: Shows two cousins hearing of a neighbour's internship: one is inspired because the steps seem reachable, the other sinks into envy.

passage:
In Leeds, Freya and Emeka shared a flat and a course. At breakfast Freya read the email out loud: their classmate had won a summer placement at a big engineering firm.
Emeka put down his toast. "How? What did she do?"
"Does it matter? She's brilliant. I'm not." Freya closed her laptop. For the rest of the day she didn't open her notes. She kept thinking of every mistake she'd made that term.
Emeka messaged the classmate. She replied: "Portfolio plus two cover letters. Happy to share mine."
He started his portfolio that evening. Freya watched from the sofa, feeling worse.

qa.q: What did the classmate win?
qa.a: She won a summer placement at a big engineering firm.

qa.q: What was Freya feeling when she closed her laptop?
qa.a: She felt envious and full of self-criticism, sure she wasn't good enough.

qa.q: What did Emeka do that turned the comparison into motivation?

qa.a: She may feel pleased and generous, happy to help others follow the same path.

grounding: Shows two students hearing the same news of a classmate's placement: one is pushed on by learning the steps, the other sinks into envy and self-criticism.

passage: The placement cell's board announced Rehana's summer internship at a design studio. Saurabh read it twice. They had been in the same studio class. She was good, but so was he. "If she can, maybe I can," he thought, and asked her in the corridor how she'd prepared. "Portfolio every weekend for three months," she said. "I'll send you my list." That night he started his first page. Near him in the reading room, another student from their class stared at the same notice on his phone, then shut it and sat without opening his books. "Some people just have it," he muttered. Saurabh noticed the difference: for him, Rehana's news felt like a path. For the other boy, it felt like a wall.

passage:
Dear Rashmi,
I owe you an honest letter. When you got the research internship in Bengaluru, I said congratulations and then went quiet for two weeks. The truth is I was jealous. I kept comparing: your marks, your professor's praise, your confidence. I spent evenings telling myself I'd never be good enough and not studying at all. Then you messaged me your application, the one that got rejected twice before it worked. That changed something. It stopped being magic and became steps. This week I emailed two professors and started my own proposal. I'm not sure I'll get anything. But I'm working again instead of sinking. Thank you for showing me the ugly drafts.
Santosh

qa.a: Santosh felt jealous and full of self-criticism, sure of never being good enough and not studying at all.

qa.q: What turned Santosh's comparison from harmful to helpful?

grounding: Shows how comparing with a friend's internship first led to envy and self-criticism, then to effort once the goal seemed reachable.
